> Participants were 45% women, 40% men, 15% transgender, predominantly white (85%), 38 years of age (SD = 9.5) and partnered or married (75%).

> For instance, in interactions with their therapists, participants were able to "notice the anxiety and the thoughts" do things "I have never done before," such as expressing their emotions, needs, or aspects of themselves that they often conceal.

> In this way, experiences during the MDMA session where participants were able to notice a difference between how they interacted with their therapist during the session, and how they typically interact with other in their daily lives, provided new learning.

power.title: Power Analysis Check
report:
::: {.callout-tip title="Learn More" collapse="true"}

Power analyses need to contain the following information to be interpretable: the type of power analysis, the statistical test, the software used, sample size, critical alpha criterion, power level, effect size, and an effect size metric. In addition, it is recommended to make sure the power analysis is reproducible (by sharing the code, or a screenshot, of the power analysis), and to provide good arguments for why the study was designed to detect an effect of this size.

For an a-priori power analysis, where the sample size is determined, reporting all information would look like:

> An a priori power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that for a Cohen's d = 0.5, an alpha level of 0.05, and a desired power level of 80% required at least 64 participants in each group.

For a sensitivity power analysis, this sentence would look like:

> A sensitivity power analysis for an independent samples t-test, conducted using the pwr.t.test function from pwr (Champely, 2020), indicated that with 64 participants in each group, and an alpha level of 0.05, a desired power level of 80% was reached for an effect size of d = 0.5.

ownership.dep_description: Background: ±3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) has positive effects on socio-emotional processing and MDMA-Assisted Therapy (MDMA-AT) showed promise for treating SAD in a previous placebo-controlled trial. Aims: Develop a preliminary estimate of clinical response and safety for MDMA-AT versus waitlist in adults with SAD. Secondary aims included refinement of a standardized psychotherapy manual and assessment of candidate therapeutic processes. Method: This randomized, open-label, wait-list controlled clinical trial recruited and enrolled 20 participants diagnosed with SAD from April, 2022 to March, 2024. They were randomly assigned to either immediate treatment with MDMA-AT or a 16-week waitlist condition followed by MDMA-AT equivalent to the immediate treatment arm. text.text: Social anxiety disorder involves intense distress or disruption due to fear of social or performance situations that involve the potential for scrutiny, judgment, embarrassment, or humiliation (American Psychiatric Association, 2022).
text.formatted: Social anxiety disorder involves intense distress or disruption due to fear of social or performance situations that involve the potential for scrutiny, judgment, embarrassment, or humiliation <ref type="bibr">(American Psychiatric Association, 2022)</ref>.

text.text: Treatment guidelines for social anxiety disorder generally recommend pharmacological intervention, typically selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and cognitive behavioral therapy (Andreoli et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Treatment guidelines for social anxiety disorder generally recommend pharmacological intervention, typically selective serotonin reuptake inhibitors, and cognitive behavioral therapy <ref type="bibr" target="#b2">(Andreoli et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: While these treatments show effectiveness compared to control or placebo conditions (Sun et al., 2025; Williams et al., 2020), treatment response (Springer et al., 2018) and care needs (Stein et al., 2021) are heterogenous.

text.text: Research on the effectiveness of psychedelic-assisted treatments for a range of mental health conditions, such as depression, post-traumatic stress disorder, and substance use disorders is growing (Dominiak et al., 2025). 3,4-methylenedioxymethamphetamine (MDMA) administered in the context of psychotherapy, termed MDMA-Assisted Therapy (MDMA-AT), has shown promising outcomes and preliminary evidence of safety for PTSD (Mitchell et al., 2021 (Mitchell et al., , 2023)), social anxiety in autistic adults (Danforth et al., 2018), and social anxiety in non-autistic adults (Luoma et al., 2026).

text.text: The effects of MDMA-which has a phenomenological profile characterized by positive mood, social connectedness, compassion, openness, sociability and emotional empathy (Bershad et al., 2016; Kamboj et al., 2018; Peled-Avron et al., 2025)-are thought to enhance the effects of psychotherapy.

text.text: This may especially be the case for people who face barriers to engaging in psychotherapy, due to their social anxiety, harsh self-criticism, or fearfulness expressing themselves openly or vulnerably in a therapeutic context (Luoma & Lear, 2021).

text.text: A key gap in the psychedelic and MDMA-AT literature is understanding the psychological processes through which treatment may exert its effects.
To date, most work has examined the role of mystical experiences, dose, and intensity of acute subjective experiences in predicting outcomes (Viljoen et al., 2026).
text.formatted: To date, most work has examined the role of mystical experiences, dose, and intensity of acute subjective experiences in predicting outcomes <ref type="bibr" target="#b56">(Viljoen et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: However, research on predictors and moderators of treatment outcomes indicates that other psychological processes of change appear to be at play, including increases in openness (Wagner et al., 2017), connectedness (Kałużna et al., 2022), ego dissolution (Kałużna et al., 2022), therapeutic alliance (Zeifman et al., 2024), and self-compassion (Fauvel et al., 2023; Zeifman et al., 2025), emotional breakthrough (Roseman et al., 2019) and decreases in experiential avoidance (Zeifman et al., 2023).

text.text: Understanding how people who undergo psychedelic-assisted therapy understand and interpret therapeutic benefits is key to advancing an understanding of how these treatments work.
In this way, qualitative work can help refine theory on psychedelic-assisted therapy processes of change and ensure their measurement aligns with and captures the spectrum of patient experiences.

Based on a qualitative thematic synthesis of 15 studies of patient experiences in psychedelic treatments, patients often reported that newfound insights, compassionate self-perspectives, feelings of interconnectedness, transcendental experiences, and accessing previously inaccessible emotional states contributed to the treatment's therapeutic benefits (Breeksema et al., 2020).

text.text: This study represents the first qualitative analysis to explore experiences of MDMA-AT for people with social anxiety disorder.
We aimed to understand what changes participants noticed following treatment, as well as what aspects of treatment, if any, they attributed to these changes.
Our analysis aimed to advance theory on how MDMA-AT is experienced by and may function for people with social anxiety disorder.
The parent study was a randomized waitlist, delayed-treatment control trial of MDMA-AT for 20 adults with social anxiety disorder (NCT05138068; Lear et al., 2023; Luoma et al., 2026).

text.text: Participants were 45% women, 40% men, 15% transgender, predominantly white (85%), 38 years of age (SD = 9.5) and partnered or married (75%).
Regarding sexual orientation, participants were 60% heterosexual, 20% bisexual, 10% gay, and 10% pansexual.
Further demographic information is available in the primary outcome paper (see Luoma et al., 2026).
text.formatted: Further demographic information is available in the primary outcome paper (see <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">Luoma et al., 2026)</ref>.

text.text: The intervention entailed three 90-minute preparation sessions, and two MDMA sessions followed each by three 90-minute integration sessions.
Resilient Pharmaceuticals Inc supplied midomafetamine (commonly referred to as MDMA), an investigational product not approved by the U.S. Food and Drug Administration.
For the first six participants, the therapeutic approach was inner-directed, guided by the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelics Studies (Mithoefer, 2017).
text.formatted: For the first six participants, the therapeutic approach was inner-directed, guided by the Multidisciplinary Association for Psychedelics Studies <ref type="bibr" target="#b41">(Mithoefer, 2017)</ref>.

text.text: For the remaining 14 participants, the team iteratively refined the manual to incorporate more active treatment elements pertaining to theorized mechanisms of action for MDMA and social anxiety disorder (Luoma et al., 2022; Luoma & Lear, 2021).
text.formatted: For the remaining 14 participants, the team iteratively refined the manual to incorporate more active treatment elements pertaining to theorized mechanisms of action for MDMA and social anxiety disorder <ref type="bibr" target="#b38">(Luoma et al., 2022;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b35">Luoma & Lear, 2021)</ref>.

text.text: These active treatment elements included exposure activities (e.g., "authenticity experiments", actively practicing desired social behaviors outside sessions) and self-compassion exercises (e.g., revisiting shame-laden memories from a compassionate vantage point, reframing experiences of shame and criticism through a compassionate lens).
The morning after each MDMA session, prior to their integration session, participants completed a 15-minute one-on-one semi-structured interview via Zoom with a research team member (AS, AS, CC).
All participants elected to participate in both interviews.
The interview guide (see Supplementary Online Materials Appendix A) consisted of open-ended questions inquiring about any potential beneficial, challenging, and harmful MDMA-AT experiences.

The domains assessed in the post-dosing interview remained the same across all participants, though additional optional follow-up prompts assessing unique aspects of the intervention were added as the treatment was iteratively developed.
For instance, after participants discussed beneficial MDMA-AT experiences, they may be prompted by the follow-up question: "Did you try any new social behaviors the session?"
Interviews were video recorded then transcribed verbatim.
We used reflexive thematic analysis (Braun & Clarke, 2019; Terry et al., 2017) to identify and interpret patterns of meaning across the dataset (the two post-dosing sessions).

text.text: Coding was abductive, as we aimed to allow participant narratives to guide theme generation without preconceived interpretations or theory, though analysis was also shaped by our interview guide (Morgan, 2020).

text.text: We adopted a phenomenological orientation, seeking to capture how participants subjectively made sense of their treatment experiences.

This was situated within a critical realist framework, which assumes that participants' accounts offer insight into their lived realities, while also recognizing that these accounts are shaped by social and cultural context, including, in the present study, the therapeutic context.
Consistent with this stance, analysis attended to both explicit (semantic) and underlying (latent) meanings in the data.
Three researchers (AS, MD, and CC) first familiarised themselves with all transcripts and shared initial reflections on patterns across the dataset in team meetings.
Feedback on preliminary themes was then garnered from another team member (JL).
Next, a team member (CC) coded all transcripts in ATLAS.ti (ATLAS.ti Scientific Software Development GmbH, 2023).

Team members (AS, MD, CC) reviewed and discussed themes iteratively through team meetings, refining interpretations and ensuring that themes were well grounded in the data while incorporating multiple analytic perspectives.
Because the analysis team collectively observed no key differences in themes between the two MDMA sessions, results are presented across the sessions.
Team members agreed that codes stabilized by participant 15, while nuance within themes continued to be refined through the remaining interviews.
Additional methodological details are presented in the Consolidated criteria for reporting qualitative research (COREQ) checklist (Tong et al., 2007) in Supplementary Online Materials Appendix B.

text.text: Engaging in reflexivity, we acknowledge that our analysis was shaped by our interest in novel mental health treatments and a pre-existing view that MDMA-AT was generally beneficial alongside a wariness of psychedelic exceptionalism.

Additionally, one researcher's perspective (CC) was likely shaped by her clinical psychology perspective and prior reading and conversation on potential mechanisms of change within MDMA-AT and another's (AS) was likely shaped by a background in contextual behavioral science.

Participant reports of change (and thus the resulting themes) were likely shaped by the specific therapeutic approach, which was developed to capitalize on MDMA's pharmacological effects, and target psychological processes underlying social anxiety disorder (Luoma & Lear, 2021; Luoma et al., 2022).

1: Healing Catalysed by Gently Facing Difficult Experiences

Participants shared the ability to gain distance from their memories, bring "curiosity" to their past experiences, and mindfully observe how events from their past influenced who they are and their patterns.

For instance, one participant described how they were able to "take a neutral point of view" while exploring memories: "It was a mixture of being curious of what I was going through or feeling at the time, like what might have caused me to act a certain way.
And it was also a mixture of holding some softness and some tenderness to-for my younger self."

(P8) Many described being able to observe themselves, their past experiences or their "younger self" or "inner child" with a sense of "compassion", "understanding", "selfforgiveness", "love", "softness" or "tenderness", as opposed to "criticism", "shame" and Through mindful observation of their life and "looking at myself more holistically", participants discovered a sense of confidence, capability, and strength.

For instance: "I'm more capable than I thought, like I'm more I guess just like stronger in some ways, like I felt able to sort of see the things that have happened to me in my life and sort of like the patterns in my life that-well clearly I must be like resilient, you know?"

All participants mentioned that during a significant part of the MDMA sessions, they felt decreased resistance or increased ease exploring parts of self, "facing painful things": "I mean, I think it helps with um sitting with uncomfortable feelings um that you might otherwise want to avoid or try to avoid."
(P10) "I had a really hard time accessing my usual kind of flood of emotions.
I was able to talk about things that would normally kind of knock me over with crying sort of matter of factly.
It was a pleasant surprise."

Through the process of engaging with the internal experiences, participants often felt a heightened sense of achievement, of "moving through material", "getting through many things" and "getting a lot done": "I ended up processing a lot of memories.
I had a lot of stuff that was just instantly coming up."

(P20) This process of "auditing" and "cataloguing" memories was experienced by participants as "beneficial", "productive" or "freeing", as they were able to examine their experiences with greater clarity and understanding: "There was a period of, I guess 4 hours and it felt like there was a cataloguing, organizing going on of memories at the time."

The overarching theme of new perspectives and insights captured participants feeling that they had a "different" or "clearer" way of understanding themselves, others or the world, one that fell "outside [their] normal thinking."
For instance: "That clarity was very-I think that was the best part.
Being able to see things very

At other times, participants described not necessarily greater clarity, but rather greater comfort with ambiguity or apparent contradictions, or a sense of duality within their experiences: "With some of these memories during a certain period of my time, I like to think of it as like all like negative, almost like it was a complete bad experience.
I don't think that's the case.
There's a lot of, like, good in those experiences too."
(P6) "I think we need pain because pain is like training for recognizing beauty.
Yeah, so pain is-in order to appreciate um what's happening inside our bodies, we actually need pain."

Participant felt that they could now understand the underlying, "deeper impact" or origins of their anxiety, "see more specifically what the problem was," "connect dots," or better understand the "root" of their struggles: Several participants shared insights into self-protective behaviors (e.g., not "letting other people love me", being "walled off", or perfectionism) that prevented them from connecting with others or perpetuated social anxiety: "I think an insight was that in kind of cutting myself off from any sort of negative critique about those things, I'm also kind of cutting myself off from any support or any positive feedback."

(P16) "Something that's kind of stopped me from expressing appreciation to people is just like feeling like it wouldn't be able to do it in the right way (…) But I feel like, you know, it's OK if it's not the right way.
It's better to express things than not express at all."

Participants gained insight into their true needs, desires, or aspects of self, often masked by anxiety: "Behind the anxiety I have these desires to speak in front of people to read, to perform, to play, maybe to have a creative outlet.
Those were some big insights."

Another participant shared the insight that "behavior patterns that I have that are causing me issues now," stem from anxiety, not an inherent part of themselves, explaining: Some participants expressed a newfound awareness of and connection to desires to connect more with others and express themselves.
For instance, one participant shared a core desire "to be seen and to be loved", explaining: "I see now why I haven't felt safe to be seen or safe to express my emotions."
Participants described a sense of oneness, expansion or greater connection to humanity, nature, the universe, or a higher power.
These experiences included a sense of unity with their external world, feeling "like the universe is inside you" (P11), and a "transcendent sort of oneness… feeling of love and connection" (P1).

Feelings of oneness and broadened attention often gave rise to greater feelings of empathy and understanding for others: "I could just see so clearly that while of course these people had individual personalities and were making choices, they were also within these larger contexts that they absolutely couldn't control.
You know, they couldn't control like, where they grew up, how their parents were, how people around them treated them."
(P5) "[I had a] greater sense of empathy and kind of openness um towards people that I've had difficulty with.
I was just trying to think of like, you know of people that cause me the most like distress [chuckles] and was able to have like warm understanding feelings towards them."
text.formatted: I was just trying to think of like, you know of people that cause me the most like distress <ref type="bibr">[chuckles]</ref> and was able to have like warm understanding feelings towards them."

text.text: Oftentimes, participants physically felt and deeply understood parts of themselves that they were only previously able to access "intellectually" and "cognitively": "I kind of understood intellectually in the past, like "Oh yeah, I can tell that I react to this in this way, and this happens", but I kind of more um felt it directly instead of like analyzing it."

There was a general desire, willingness or ability expressed by participants to explore and experience emotions that are generally suppressed and harder to access when not under the influence of MDMA, such as anger, grief difficult emotions, or painful memories.

For instance, one participant described experiencing a "seething hot rage kind of feeling", explaining: "I really don't like being an angry person, so um it was difficult to feel a lot of anger, and also a very, like, despairing like depression (…) I don't want to experience them, but um I was trying to just experience them."

(P1) This embodied experiencing created vulnerability which could feel challenging but was also felt as "cathartic", "releasing" or "beneficial" or which created a deep sense of relief, purpose and freedom.
For instance: "It feels like a lot of stuck emotional business has been swept away and there's an opening there."
(P2) "So it was like a huge relief.
It was in my mind, a significant moment of moving past something that's been haunting me for a long time."
One participant described the experience of "releasing" as having a physical manifestation: "At one point out my jaw was like going, shaking.
Like, I think I was releasing some stuff.
Yeah, I have no, no lower back pain this morning.
It's gone."

Participants described an array of embodied positive states, in which they experienced feeling "at home", "connected", "safe" "calm, steady", "solid", "good and relaxed" and "in harmony with the physical body."
For instance: "I felt really open and I felt really safe.
I felt surprisingly calm the whole time, which is not what I expected at all [chuckles]."
text.formatted: I felt surprisingly calm the whole time, which is not what I expected at all <ref type="bibr">[chuckles]</ref>."

text.text: Other participants described positive physical experiences enduring after the MDMA session, such as feeling "lighter."

For instance, one participant described no longer feeling pain due to arthritis in their hand and back, and a "persistent back thing around my SI joint and on my left side": "I don't feel that pain anymore, and it's so weird, I'm sure it will come back.
And it hasn't come back and it usually like will come back overnight...

It's having me wonder if there's like a muscle relaxing quality to it that then allowed that stretch to kind of like work and like release the muscle so my skeletal body could like get back into place or something?"

Other participants experienced a felt sense of confidence, worthiness and of feeling selfcompassionate, "lovable" and "happy": "I just felt like this over all sense of like belief in myself and (…) um I guess just confidence in myself to kind of change my life in the ways that I want to rather than kind of being afraid to do it."

As another example, one participant described generally having a harsh, negative self-image, but feelings "the complete opposite" during the MDMA session: During the MDMA sessions, participants experienced greater ease or ability to express themselves and practice new interpersonal behaviors that beyond the MDMA session would have felt "negative", "scary", "shameful", "challenging," or "uncomfortable."
Several participants noticed an increased sense of authenticity and self-expression.

It was "easier to talk," "more natural to share things that made me feel vulnerable," and there was a greater willingness to be "honest," "vulnerable," and "trusting" with the therapists: The ability to share more freely during the session was perceived as a new, beneficial or "powerful" experience, enabling the participants to move beyond topics they "wouldn't necessarily have wanted to talk about" and thus "go in depth" and move beyond what they are able to do in prior therapy: "I definitely was able to talk more with my therapist about like previous events that I hadn't really been able to go in depth on (…) but like far less challenging than it would have been just in a normal like therapy session."

The MDMA sessions also afforded participants the opportunity to see their social anxiety played out in real time in relationship with the therapists and practice relating to or working through their anxiety in constructive ways.

For instance, in interactions with their therapists, participants were able to "notice the anxiety and the thoughts" do things "I have never done before," such as expressing their emotions, needs, or aspects of themselves that they often conceal.

This vulnerable self-expression allowed participants to work through their social anxiety in real time, which felt "huge", "very productive", "cathartic", "beneficial" and "impactful", or led to new insights: "I arrived at this place of like-actually, it actually doesn't matter if they like me or not (…) But actually I in that moment felt really calm and at peace in my body. " (P12) Interactions such as communicating openly with the therapists and doing desired activities that participants generally avoided due to shame or anxiety (e.g., drawing, asking for hugs) were considered new corrective experiences.

text.text: In this way, experiences during the MDMA session where participants were able to notice a difference between how they interacted with their therapist during the session, and how they typically interact with other in their daily lives, provided new learning.
For instance: "It's something I would never, ever do, and I was worried about asking leading up to it, but at the moment I just felt like that was the right thing to do.
And I asked them to hold my hands and so I feel like those were really helpful things that helped me move through things that may have been holding me back."
Experiences from the MDMA sessions equipped participants with helpful metaphors, symbols, insights, new ways of thinking, or broadened access to emotional states.

In this way, the MDMA session could serve as a frame of reference to revisit after the session, offering participants hope and a willingness or motivation to practice new ways of being with themselves and others.

For instance, one participant described an intention to "carry or at Another participant described a desire to continue practicing behaviors they practiced with their therapists in session, such as reading in front of others, and caring for themselves: "You know, a little bit more anxiety is in my body now, of course, now that I'm not on the medicine.
But I still feel really close to like, things I want to change."

The powerful somatic sensations described in Theme 3 appeared to function as an anchor some could return to and were associated with a desire to revisit feeling such as sureness, confidence, ease, and openness outside of the MDMA sessions.

This study drew on qualitative interviews of 20 participants who underwent MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder, adding depth to the quantitative findings reported in the parent study (Luoma et al., 2026) by exploring participants' descriptions of their treatment experiences, the changes they experienced after MDMA sessions and the aspects of MDMA-AT they felt were most instrumental to beneficial changes.
text.formatted: This study drew on qualitative interviews of 20 participants who underwent MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder, adding depth to the quantitative findings reported in the parent study <ref type="bibr" target="#b36">(Luoma et al., 2026)</ref> by exploring participants' descriptions of their treatment experiences, the changes they experienced after MDMA sessions and the aspects of MDMA-AT they felt were most instrumental to beneficial changes.

text.text: Overall, participants described how facing difficult experiences and emotions with curiosity, mindfulness and compassion catalysed healing and new understandings.
Fully experiencing painful emotions allowed participants to move from stagnation towards greater flexibility.
Participants described positive states (e.g., interconnectedness, social safety) as more of an embodied or felt-sense experience, versus an intellectualized understanding.
Moments of vulnerable self-expression with therapists were important to participants, creating opportunities for relational learning to unfold during sessions.
Together, MDMA session experiences appeared to provide a salient "anchor" that participants could return to after sessions in their ongoing growth process.
All participants described reduced barriers to examining difficult internal experiences during at least one of the MDMA sessions.
In contending with these difficult internal experiences, participants were able to perceive their memories, behaviors, and thought patterns as a curious, compassionate observer.

The mindful distance enabled shifts from shame and self-judgement toward greater self-compassion and understanding, helping participants cultivate a more holistic self-awareness, greater self-confidence and greater selfefficacy.
Mindfulness and compassion practices have shown efficacy for social anxiety (Liu et al., 2021).
text.formatted: Mindfulness and compassion practices have shown efficacy for social anxiety <ref type="bibr" target="#b33">(Liu et al., 2021)</ref>.

text.text: Yet, many participants described difficulty applying such practices prior to the MDMA sessions, suggesting that MDMA may enhance people's ability to access and thus practice adopting mindful, curious and compassionate perspectives.

The observed enhanced capacity to tolerate and move through challenging internal experiences is consistent with prior MDMA-AT for PTSD research, in which participants similarly described enhanced willingness to experience and explore, rather than suppress, uncomfortable emotions, which facilitated shifts in self-perception, including greater self-love and self-forgiveness (Barone et al., 2019; Godes et al., 2023).

text.text: Participants all also described a general broadening in their perspectives of themselves and others.
Many described how reduced anxiety during MDMA sessions helped them understand their true desires, which had previously been masked by social anxiety.
This parallels prior MDMA-AT for PTSD work, in which participants disentangled past traumatic events from their self-concept, and connected with "lost parts" of themselves (Godes et al., 2023).

text.text: Our findings lend support to conceptualizations of authenticity as multidimensional, entailing self-awareness, unbiased processing of self-relevant information, behavior that is congruent with one's values, preferences and needs, and a relational dimension (Kernis & Goldman, 2006).

text.text: Participants described each of these dimensions of authenticity as interconnected: more objective, mindful observation enabled greater self-awareness, and deepened connection with the authentic self was led to greater clarity around social needs (e.g., to be seen) and greater desires to practice new social behaviors to meet those needs (e.g., vulnerable self-expression).
Clinically, our findings suggest that authenticity may serve as a valuable social anxiety treatment target.

MDMA-AT may be particularly well-suited to target authenticity processes; MDMA appears to facilitate mindful, unbiased observation of the self, while the therapeutic context may promote and reinforce social insights.

In prior MDMA-AT studies, participants generally describe a newfound ability to reason through past experiences, leading to therapeutically beneficial insight that can be readily articulated (Barone et al., 2019; Godes et al., 2023).
text.formatted: In prior MDMA-AT studies, participants generally describe a newfound ability to reason through past experiences, leading to therapeutically beneficial insight that can be readily articulated <ref type="bibr" target="#b3">(Barone et al., 2019;</ref> <ref type="bibr" target="#b24">Godes et al., 2023)</ref>.

text.text: In the present study, participants not only described newfound clarity and insights, but also a mode of knowing that transcended the intellectual.
Beliefs they had previously only been able to access intellectually (e.g., that they were lovable) were felt directly under the acute effects of MDMA and subsequently.

Embodied experiences of self-worthiness (e.g., "I was just this beautiful, happy person") countered participants' typical shame-based ways of viewing themselves and may have served as corrective experiences in relation to a shame-bound sense of self.

Participants also often described a distinct sense of calm and safety within the body, which facilitated greater comfort and feelings of safeness in interpersonal interactions, mirroring feelings of social safety and comfort described in prior MDMA-AT research (Barone et al., 2019; Godes et al., 2023).

text.text: Experiences of interconnectedness and oneness also stood out as impactful embodied states for participants.
With classic psychedelics, self-transcendent experiences often are characterized by both feelings of unity and a sense of ego/self-dissolution (Nour et al., 2016).
text.formatted: With classic psychedelics, self-transcendent experiences often are characterized by both feelings of unity and a sense of ego/self-dissolution <ref type="bibr" target="#b44">(Nour et al., 2016)</ref>.

text.text: In contrast, MDMA-occasioned self-transcendent experiences in this study were only characterized by broadened interconnection, suggesting a distinct experiential quality.

Future work would benefit from assessing distinct dimensions of self-transcendent experiences to aid in advancing the phenomenology of distinct psychedelics, and predictors of distinct selftranscendental experiences.

In our quantitative study with the same sample, self-transcendent experiences related to heightened connection, but not ego dissolution, predicted wellbeingrelated outcomes (belonging, gratitude, purpose in life) (Chwyl et al., 2026).

text.text: This finding adds to a growing body of work finding this same pattern: self-transcendent experiences characterized by heightened connection are specifically associated with beneficial outcomes (Chwyl, Angelica, et al., 2025; Cova & Abatista, 2025; Kałużna et al., 2022; Tyson et al., 2022; Yaden, 2020).

text.text: Our findings also provide insights into how transcendental experiences may give rise to benefits: participants described how experiences of love, compassion, and unity gave rise to greater empathy, understanding, and nuance in their perspectives, motivating them to deepen connections with themselves, others and their community.
In addition to describing embodied positive states, participants also often reported greater ability to experience typically inaccessible challenging states (e.g., suppressed anger).
This led to what participants felt was an "emotional release" or "catharsis."
Often, participants described emotional relief experiences as intertwined with a felt physical release (e.g., MDMA as having a "muscle relaxing" quality).

For two participants, physical pain relief endured beyond the acute effects of MDMA, contrasting most prior qualitative work instead focusing exclusively on emotional pain (for an exception, see : Godes et al., 2023; Watts et al., 2017).

text.text: Our work adds to a small but growing literature on the potential for psychedelics (Robinson et al., 2024) and MDMA (Christie et al., 2022; Gasser et al., 2025) to treat certain types of pain.

text.text: While the mechanisms through which psychedelics may influence pain remain largely theoretical (Castellanos et al., 2020), our results suggest that broadened emotional access may play a role.

text.text: This is consistent with work suggesting that emotional processing treatments, which engage both the somatic and mental experiencing of an emotion, may be particularly effective in reducing chronic pain in individuals with trauma and psychosocial conflicts (Lumley et al., 2021).

text.text: Participants described the importance of not only approaching internal experiences but also practicing new behaviors in-session, such as disclosing material they habitually concealed, expressing emotions and needs directly, or asking for physical contact.

For instance, one participant, attending closely to how the therapists were perceiving them, arrived at the realization that "it actually doesn't matter if they like me or not" while feeling calm and at peace in their body.

MDMA's acute effects, such as reduced anxiety, and heightened trust, emotional openness and sociability (Bershad et al., 2016; Kamboj et al., 2018), may have made these behaviors possible for participants who could not otherwise attempt them.

text.text: Setting likely amplified pharmacological effects, as participants reported that the therapeutic setting felt safe, attuned and flexible, which likely facilitated them facing difficulties, fully experiencing emotions, and more openly discussing experiences.
MDMA experiences functioned not only as a catalyst for healing, but also as an anchor for participants to return to thereafter.
Some participants were able to carry forward useful symbols, metaphors, or new frameworks for self-understanding.

Others, building upon progress and momentum established from the MDMA sessions, described greater selfefficacy or desire to try new social activities, cultivate community, or express themselves authentically.

These findings build on prior psychedelic-assisted therapy literature, in which participants described bringing forward new modes of thinking, symbolic frameworks and renewed motivation into new actions in life following psychedelic use (Barone et al., 2019; Camlin et al., 2018; Watts et al., 2017).

text.text: However, our analysis also yielded a dimension not commonly described in previous reports: participants expressed a desire to not only revisit cognitive insights but also reconnect with embodied states deeply felt during the sessions.

While participants expressed a strong desire to remember and revisit these feelings, some expressed uncertainty around how to "preserve that state" or "recapture that image and that feeling", such as a positive self-image, ease or less guardedness.
Overall, our work extends the literature on how participants experience change within psychedelic-assisted therapy to the context of MDMA-AT for social anxiety disorder.

Prior qualitative studies have found many similarities in how participants describe their process of change across different psychedelics (e.g., classic psychedelics, MDMA, ketamine) and disorders (Breeksema et al., 2020).

text.text: Together, these results suggest that certain dimensions of how participants experience therapeutic change may transcend psychopharmacology and diagnostic boundaries.
At the same time, other findings, such as how heavily interpersonal dimensions featured in themes, may be especially pertinent to a social anxiety population.

For a condition characterized by social struggles and disconnection, interpersonal experiences within treatment (e.g., social insights, embodied feelings of social safety and interconnection, identifying and practicing social behaviors) may be key facilitators of change.

In Theme 4 (Learning New Relational Patterns through Vulnerable Self-Expression), interpersonal experiences not only appeared to facilitate change but the therapeutic relationship itself also served as the arena in which change occurred.
For people with social anxiety disorder, therapists themselves are instances of the feared situation: people who are watching, listening, and potentially judging.

The MDMA sessions appeared to function as a form of in vivo exposure, or a live behavioral experiment, in which participants could notice their anxiety and anticipatory thoughts as they arose, act in new ways, and observe what actually happened.
Feared predictions of rejection, judgment or humiliation could be tested and disconfirmed in real-time by the therapists' actual responses (e.g., warmth, acceptance).

Such real-time interpersonal learning aligns with inhibitory learning and memory reconsolidation accounts of exposure, in which "expectancy violations" are conceptualized as key mechanisms of change (Craske et al., 2014; Luoma et al., 2022).

text.text: New relational learning may be especially central to psychedelic-assisted therapy with social anxiety disorder, or struggles involving interpersonal or betrayal dimensions.

Our results also highlighted the centrality of emotional embodiment, which allowed for transformative experiences with positive emotions (e.g., feeling free, safe, loving), and for wisdom to be felt ("implanted in a physical way").
To continue their therapeutic progress, participants expressed a desire to reconnect with embodied states deeply felt during MDMA sessions.

Our results emphasize the importance of therapeutic approaches that go beyond intellectual discussion and instead center in-the-moment felt emotional experience, such as emotion-focused (Greenberg, 2004), Gestalt (Yontef & Jacobs, 2005), and mindfulnessfocused traditions (Kabat-Zinn, 2003).

text.text: Our findings also spotlight the importance of positive affect: participants not only found it impactful to confront painful content but also found tremendous benefit in experientially feeling states that they often found difficult to access (e.g., feeling free, safe, loved).
Such experiences were described as contributing to benefits well beyond social anxiety reduction, including greater self-understanding, connection with self and others, and wellbeing.

Clinically, our results support therapeutic approaches that incorporate positive psychology principles (e.g., savoring, gratitude, positive imagery, leveraging strengths, engaging in pleasurable and rewarding activities, strengthening relationships) and target not just symptom reduction, but also wellbeing (Carr et al., 2021; Craske et al., 2023).

text.text: Given the nonlinearity of integration and healing (Chwyl, Elvenes, et al., 2025), how participants' understanding of their experiences changes over time, and after treatment concludes, remains an interesting open question.

text.text: It's important to acknowledge that the present themes unfolded within, and were shaped by, the particular context of the current treatment.

Participants referenced how elements of set and setting-such as music, eye shades, preparation, caffeine/food intake, ceremony/ritual, and broader life circumstances-facilitated or complicated their experience.

Participants frequently discussed synergy between MDMA and the therapeutic relationship, aligning with prior qualitative (Breeksema et al., 2020) and quantitative work (Zeifman et al., 2024) that has highlighted the centrality of the therapeutic relationship and nonpharmacological factors in facilitating beneficial psychedelic outcomes.

text.text: Findings from this study cannot isolate the contribution of MDMA's pharmacological properties from that of the therapeutic protocol itself.

A key aspect of the study that likely influenced the observed themes was the therapeutic approach, which may have influenced what experiences felt salient and important to participants, and the language they used to describe their experiences within interviews.

For instance, therapists provided psychoeducation around shame-based conceptualizations of social anxiety, the importance of creating opportunities for expectancy violations, and memory reconsolidation (Luoma et al., 2025).
text.formatted: For instance, therapists provided psychoeducation around shame-based conceptualizations of social anxiety, the importance of creating opportunities for expectancy violations, and memory reconsolidation <ref type="bibr" target="#b37">(Luoma et al., 2025)</ref>.

text.text: The therapeutic approach also featured several positive psychology principles, such as savoring exercises, noticing past/present moments of social safety, and encouraging engagement in more value-aligned actions, which may have shaped the thematic emphasis on positive experiences, alongside MDMA's pharmacological effects.

Finally, compared to most prior psychedelic and MDMA-AT studies, therapists adopted a more active role through in-session experiential exercises, such as guided imagery and "authenticity experiments."

Moreover, therapists encouraged participants to capitalize on the heightened post-MDMA window for learning through homework, social-based goals, and revisiting important moments/feelings from the sessions.
This active therapeutic stance may have influenced a range of themes, though especially themes involving interpersonal learning.

Supporting this hypothesis, Themes 4 (Learning New Relational Patterns through Vulnerable Self-Expression) appeared more unique to the current study, surfacing less in prior work (Breeksema et al., 2020).

text.text: Given the likely influence of this trial's more directive protocol elements, future MDMA-AT approaches for social anxiety disorder may benefit from deliberately incorporating structured components such as exposure and compassionbased exercises, and from training therapists to work directly with the in-session relationship, such as in functional analytical psychotherapy, where the in-the-moment therapeutic relationship is considered the primary vehicle for promoting lasting change (Kohlenberg & Tsai, 2007).

text.text: Limitations of this study include a sample that is homogenous in certain dimensions (85% white), and highly screened (exclusions included psychotic disorder, bipolar 1, autism spectrum disorder, active eating disorders, substance use disorders, personality disorders (except avoidant), current PTSD, serious suicide risk, and recent ketamine or antidepressant use).

It's also important to note that while the current paper does not present adverse or challenging experiences, these will be reported in a separate study (participants commonly shared challenging yet beneficial experiences and infrequently reported adverse experiences).
The MDMA-AT experiences presented in this paper may therefore not generalize to certain groups, and rates of challenging or adverse experiences may be greater with a more representative sample.

MDMA-AT appeared to serve as a catalyst for gently facing, deeply feeling, and experiencing emotions, which enabled both new perspectives and an embodied form of knowing that transcended an intellectual understanding.

MDMA's pharmacological effects and the therapeutic protocol, designed specifically to capitalize on those effects in service of a particular conceptualization of social anxiety disorder, appeared to work synergistically to enable salient moments of connection, compassion and authentic self-expression.

In this way, MDMA-AT may facilitate key experiences that are important for therapeutic change, yet hard to access for people with social anxiety: a curious and compassionate stance towards difficult internal experiences, and experiences of genuine acceptance and social safety that counter expectations of rejection or shame.

These findings connect MDMA-AT to established literatures on exposure and inhibitory learning, relational and corrective learning in psychotherapy, and experiential and emotion-focused psychotherapy, suggesting that the therapeutic significance of MDMA-AT may lie in part in making processes already central to effective treatment accessible to those who struggle most to engage them.
